S6.note: Why only one blue tip? GenBank has almost no RPB1 for this group: the P. natalensis holotype PQ317409 is the only member here (chuxiongensis's single RPB1 was not in the paper's figure; maluti has none). That holotype RPB1 is itself a short, partial, UNVERIFIED 591 bp fragment, so it cannot anchor a distinct lineage — our specimen pairs directly with it (bootstrap 100), but the pair sits next to P. cubensis rather than forming a separate clade. RPB1 is the least-resolving of the loci for this group; EF1α and RPB2, which have fuller references, place the specimen inside the group cleanly.

S7.note: One tip, but a dikaryon underneath. Our specimen is a dikaryon (n+n), so its single-copy RPB2 actually exists as two haplotypes — nucleus A and nucleus B, differing by 12 SNPs / 0.61% (recovered by read-phasing). Only one specimen star is plotted here (the polished assembly consensus): adding the two near-identical, pre-polish haplotypes as extra tips biases the clustering — they attract each other and the missing data (~100 Ns each) pulls them toward the outgroup. Both phased haplotype sequences are provided in full on the Assembly & decon tab (Pnat_specimen_RPB2_haplotypeA / B) and documented in ASSEMBLY.md.

notes: Flye reported an estimated 147× coverage, but that is throughput ÷ 60 Mb target size — a bookkeeping figure, not measured depth. Because most reads turn out to be bacterial, true on-target fungal depth is lower and is being measured by mapping reads back to the clean draft.
A haploid Psilocybe genome is ~47–50 Mb. This draft is roughly 3× that: a dikaryon (two nuclei whose alleles partly assemble as parallel contigs) plus heavy bacterial contamination — separated below.
